__map_ecological__.name: Ecological Conservation Priorities
__map_ecological__.description: Every contributing layer combined into a single map of ecological importance. Each area takes the importance of the highest-ranked layer covering it, so overlap never inflates a score. Hover any area to see which layers contribute there.

__map_agricultural__.name: Agricultural Conservation Priorities
__map_agricultural__.description: Thetford's important farmland soils, ranked by NRCS crop-production score and whether the land is open today: top-rated soil on open land ranks highest, productive soil elsewhere lowest, the other two in between. The layers never overlap; hover any area to see which applies.

custom_3b424511.name: Amphibian Road Crossings
custom_3b424511.goal: Keep spring migration routes between wintering forest and breeding pools passable, and keep the roadside habitat at those spots intact.
custom_3b424511.motivation: Thetford's 2025 wildlife road crossing study found 24 biologically active amphibian crossings totaling 3.7 miles, with eight species recorded. Two are Species of Greatest Conservation Need: spotted salamander, at eight crossings, and four-toed salamander (ranked S3, uncommon in Vermont) at one. Adults cross on a handful of wet nights each spring, so a single busy stretch of road can erase a local population. See the Thetford Conservation Commission for the full inventory.

custom_f986b655.name: Confirmed Vernal Pools
custom_f986b655.goal: Protect pools with confirmed breeding activity together with the forest immediately around them.
custom_f986b655.motivation: Fishless seasonal pools are the main breeding habitat for wood frogs and for Vermont's mole salamanders — spotted, blue-spotted and Jefferson — which breed nowhere else. The animals spend most of the year in the surrounding forest, not the water, so protecting the pool alone does not work. Vermont Fish & Wildlife manages that forest out to 600 ft (Wildlife Habitat Management: A Landowner’s Guide). The 600 ft outer zone is the buffer mapped here. Pool locations come from the Vermont Vernal Pool Atlas.

custom_c2ea57e7.name: Natural Communities
custom_c2ea57e7.goal: Protect the rare and uncommon natural community types confirmed in town.
custom_c2ea57e7.motivation: Vermont recognizes 97 wetland and upland natural community types and conserving good examples of each is a cornerstone of the state's strategy for biological diversity (Vermont Fish & Wildlife natural community fact sheets). This layer holds the rare (S2) and uncommon (S3) types mapped in Thetford: Wet Clayplain Forest and Sugar Maple Riverine Forest on the glacial clays of the valley floors, an Intermediate Fen, Northern Hardwood Seepage Forest and Alluvial Shrub Swamp. Others are known to occur but have not yet been mapped. Small in acreage, disproportionate in value. Records come from the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory.

custom_0cf3cd91.name: Threatened Species
custom_0cf3cd91.goal: Protect documented habitat for species listed as threatened or endangered.
custom_0cf3cd91.motivation: The map shows ten recorded occurrences of species protected under Vermont or federal endangered species law — nine animals and one plant. Four are listed federally as well as by the state; six by the state alone. The state does not publish which species each occurrence is, and the areas drawn are generalized habitat rather than exact locations, both deliberately, so that rare species cannot be tracked down from a public map (Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory). Separately, Thetford's Natural Resource Inventory documents which listed species occur in town: three bat species — Northern Long-eared Bat, now federally endangered after white-nose syndrome cut its numbers by 97–100% range-wide (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service), Little Brown Bat and Eastern Small-footed Bat — along with the federally endangered Dwarf Wedgemussel in the Connecticut River and the state-threatened plant sweet coltsfoot. The bats spread across town's forests, wetlands and riverbanks from mid-April through October, which is why the state asks landowners to avoid cutting trees during those months. Listings from Vermont Fish & Wildlife.
custom_0cf3cd91.how_built: Occurrences in the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory (public version, data current to October 2026) of species listed as threatened or endangered by Vermont, the federal government, or both. Shapes are drawn exactly as the state publishes them, with no added buffer. Most are circles around a single observation, sized to how precisely it was located; the state notes a population may extend beyond what is mapped (Natural Heritage data guidelines).

custom_0a14cdde.name: Top Tier Crossings
custom_0a14cdde.goal: Keep passable the road segments that cut through the regional forest network.
custom_0a14cdde.motivation: These are the mapped wildlife crossings that fall inside one of Vermont Conservation Design's highest priority connectivity blocks — where a road cuts across a corridor running well beyond town, so the crossing carries more than local traffic in wildlife terms. Thetford sits in two such corridors: a north–south band along the east side of Vermont, and an east–west link from the Green Mountains to the White Mountains. Keeping forest cover on both shoulders is what maintains passage (Vermont Conservation Design; 2025 Thetford wildlife road crossing study).

custom_2bbc6497.name: Other Wetlands
custom_2bbc6497.goal: Treat every other mapped wetland and its 50 ft margin as land where change needs care.
custom_2bbc6497.motivation: Wetlands store floodwater, filter runoff and support a disproportionate share of Vermont's rare species. Thetford's are mostly small, common types, easy to lose one at a time. Every state-mapped wetland in town is Class II, so most work in one or its 50 ft buffer needs a permit under the Vermont Wetland Rules (Vermont DEC). Vermont has lost as much as 35% of its original wetlands (Vermont DEC).
custom_2bbc6497.how_built: The state's wetland inventory (2024) plus wetlands Arrowwood Environmental mapped in 2011 that the state hasn't, minus Significant Wetlands, buffered 50 ft. The 2011-only areas are advisory: places to check before work. Areas Arrowwood rated low-confidence, farm fields and man-made ponds are left out.

custom_77a73964.name: Highest Priority Connectivity Blocks
custom_77a73964.goal: Keep the forest network unfragmented, especially along the edges where blocks meet.
custom_77a73964.motivation: This is the backbone of Vermont's forest network that lets animals move across the state and into New Hampshire and Québec. It matters for daily movement, for young animals dispersing to find territory, for genetic exchange between populations, and for species shifting range as the climate warms. It covers about half of Thetford, so read it as the background the finer-scale layers sit inside rather than a designation on any one site; that is why it sits in the middle tier here despite the state calling it highest priority. The goal is to avoid permanently fragmenting these blocks (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).

custom_6c658a98.name: Top-Rated Soils, Open Land
custom_6c658a98.goal: Keep the town's best farmland that is already open available for farming.
custom_6c658a98.motivation: The soils the NRCS scores highest for crop production: agricultural value groups 1 and 2, with relative values of 100 and 97 on a 100-point scale (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils). These are already open land, so they can be farmed now without clearing. Open land is a field the town's inventory mapped from 2016 aerial imagery: hay, pasture, corn, other crops, and grassy openings of at least an acre, some of which may be large lawns (Thetford Natural Resource Inventory, 2021). These open fields also carry grassland birds that have declined regionally, including bobolink and eastern meadowlark, which nest successfully only where mowing waits until after August 1 (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).

custom_d324ef92.name: Second Tier Crossings
custom_d324ef92.goal: Keep the town's remaining road crossings permeable where habitat continues on both sides.
custom_d324ef92.motivation: The full set of wildlife crossings identified in the town inventory. Crossings that also fall inside the regional connectivity network appear in the top tier as well, and the map shows each area at its highest tier. Individually lower stakes, but collectively they are what keeps the town permeable at a local scale by letting animals reach feeding, breeding and overwintering habitat within Thetford rather than only through it. From the 2025 Thetford wildlife road crossing study.

custom_b38dc1ed.name: Productive Soils, Open Land
custom_b38dc1ed.goal: Keep good farmland that is already open available for farming.
custom_b38dc1ed.motivation: Important farmland soils with lower NRCS scores: agricultural value groups 3 to 7, with relative values from 84 down to 57 (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils). They include much of the town's prime soil, which the NRCS scores below its best soil of statewide importance. These are already open fields in the town's inventory, mapped from 2016 aerial imagery (Thetford Natural Resource Inventory, 2021), so they rank alongside top-rated soil that isn't open: one is the better soil, the other is ready to farm. These open fields also carry grassland birds that have declined regionally, including bobolink and eastern meadowlark, which nest successfully only where mowing waits until after August 1 (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).

custom_65d165d2.name: Other Top-Rated Soils
custom_65d165d2.goal: Keep the town's best farmland soils available, including where the land isn't open today.
custom_65d165d2.motivation: Soils in the NRCS's two highest agricultural value groups, with relative values of 100 and 97, that the town's inventory did not map as an open field, such as forest. They rank below open top-rated soil because farming them would first mean clearing it, but the soil is no less capable: the NRCS groups soils by their characteristics, limitations and potential for crop production, assuming any corrective measures they need, such as drainage, can be applied (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils).

custom_84edb850.name: Other Productive Soils
custom_84edb850.goal: Keep good farmland soils available for the long term.
custom_84edb850.motivation: Soils in agricultural value groups 3 to 7 that the town's inventory did not map as an open field, such as forest. They rank lowest here on both counts — a lower crop-production score, and land that would need clearing to farm — but every one is rated prime or of statewide importance (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils), and Vermont's Act 250 reviews soils of prime, statewide and local importance under Criterion 9(B), so they remain a conservation target. Thetford has no soils of local importance, so the four layers in this map cover every soil the NRCS rates as important farmland in town.

custom_bb4680ce.name: Significant Wetlands
custom_bb4680ce.goal: Avoid any development, clearing, filling or drainage in Thetford's rare, uncommon and state-significant wetlands.
custom_bb4680ce.motivation: Wetlands the town cannot replace: rare types such as the intermediate fen at Gillette Swamp, the wet clayplain forest at Connant Swamp and the sugar maple floodplain forest at Post Mills, every uncommon (S3) type, from spruce–fir–tamarack swamps to alluvial shrub swamps, and the best examples of common ones. Rare wetlands depend on particular soils, water chemistry and groundwater flow that can't be rebuilt once disturbed, so the aim is avoidance, not careful use. Vermont tracks them through its Natural Heritage Inventory.
custom_bb4680ce.how_built: Wetlands rated state-significant in Arrowwood Environmental's 2011 town inventory or by the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory, or of a community type ranked rare or uncommon (S1–S3) today, buffered 50 ft as the Vermont Wetland Rules do for Class II wetlands.

custom_0d7d7d49.name: Riparian Connectivity
custom_0d7d7d49.goal: Keep river and stream corridors forested, connected, and free to flood and meander.
custom_0d7d7d49.motivation: Riparian land does double duty: habitat for mink, otter, beaver and wood turtle, and the main connective tissue of an otherwise fragmented landscape. Forested banks stabilize soil, store floodwater, filter sediment and nutrients, and shade streams against warming. Vermont Conservation Design finds the corridor width needed for wildlife travel varies from about 100 ft on small streams to 600 ft or more on larger rivers, split either side of the water (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report). The area shown here is the state's mapped riparian connectivity network in Thetford.

custom_0ce97644.name: Other Rare Species
custom_0ce97644.goal: Protect documented habitat for rare species that are not legally listed.
custom_0ce97644.motivation: Vermont ranks species S1–S3 when they are known from only a handful to about a hundred places in the state; many are at the edge of their range or tied to scarce habitats. They have no legal protection unless listed, which makes local attention matter more. Thetford has thirteen recorded occurrences: seven animals and six plants. As with listed species, the state withholds which species each one is.
custom_0ce97644.how_built: Occurrences in the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory (public version, data current to October 2026) of rare species not listed by Vermont or federally. Shapes are drawn exactly as the state publishes them, with no added buffer. Most are circles around a single observation, sized to how precisely it was located; the state notes a population may extend beyond what is mapped (Natural Heritage data guidelines).

custom_485e642b.name: Uncommon Species
custom_485e642b.goal: Keep the habitat of Thetford's uncommon species in mind when land changes.
custom_485e642b.motivation: Uncommon species are not yet rare, but are limited in Vermont by scarce or shrinking habitat, and are the ones most likely to become rare next. Thetford has fourteen recorded occurrences: eleven animals and three plants. The state withholds which species each one is.
custom_485e642b.how_built: Occurrences in the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory's uncommon species layer (public version, data current to October 2026). Shapes are drawn exactly as the state publishes them, with no added buffer. Most are circles around a single observation, sized to how precisely it was located; the state notes a population may extend beyond what is mapped (Natural Heritage data guidelines).

custom_79610eba.name: Priority Connectivity Blocks
custom_79610eba.goal: Keep the rest of Thetford's forest network unfragmented.
custom_79610eba.motivation: The forest blocks the state rates Priority rather than Highest Priority are still part of the network that lets animals move across Vermont: they fill in between the larger blocks and keep the whole connected. Fragmenting them with roads or development narrows the routes wildlife have left (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).
